title: The Door Is Unlocked
synopsis: Six months after the bullet and the lateral array. Pixel has built a practice, a kitchen, a music collection, and a roof. Kyle has held the line — friendly, present, exactly far enough away that nothing she could lose could be used against her. She figures it out one Sunday, on the roof, with a soldering iron in one hand and a coffee in the other, and decides that the figuring-out doesn't require an answer. The book ends where Pixel began: at a window, looking out, at home.
html:
# The Door Is Unlocked

The roof of The Pivot was not, technically, accessible.

The building had been built in an era when access to a roof was a thing the city assumed people would not want, and the access hatch above the second-floor stairwell had been welded shut sometime around 2160 by a maintenance contractor who had since died and been buried by his nephew. The hatch had been re-opened, at some point, by a tenant whose name nobody now remembered, with a torch and a steady hand and a willingness to argue with three landlords across forty years that *no, you cannot reseal the hatch, the hatch is precedent now, the hatch is grandfathered.*

Mr. Adamu had inherited the argument. Mr. Adamu had also inherited his predecessor's quiet pragmatism about which fights to lose. The hatch was open. The roof was a thing.

Pixel went up there on Sundays.

It was Sunday. It was October. The light over GLMZ in October had a particular quality — the ferrocement wave to the west caught the late sun and threw it back up the lake corridor as a wide low coral that touched everything south-facing on the second story, including the roof of The Pivot, and turned the building's pigeons briefly into the most flattered pigeons in the western world.

She was on her bench, which she had hauled up four months ago across two trips. She had a soldering iron in one hand. She had a coffee in the other. She had an enormous sweater that was *not* the heathered grey, because the heathered grey was sacred and reserved for Maeve; this was the burgundy one, the *secondary* sweater, the one she wore when she wanted to feel like the burgundy version of herself. The boots were on. They had finally fit, eight months ago, and the leather had welcomed her in the particular way leather did when it agreed to be yours, and she did not, anymore, take them off in the unit unless the floor specifically required it.

The music was in her ears, both ears, because she had finally fixed the right earbud — *years* ago, she had fixed it, a hundred and seven Sundays ago, in fact — and the song that was playing was the old American song from before the Centennial, the one with the road, the one her mother had hummed at the stove. She had it on a loop because she was working with one hand and the loop did not require new attention. It was a song for the inside of a habit.

Somewhere below her, in 2F, Kyle was — she knew, because she had been doing the listening she did without trying for years — *not* home. He had been gone since Friday. He would come back tonight or tomorrow. He would come back hurt or tired or both. She would know within ninety seconds of his footfall on the stairs. She would offer; he would accept or not; either was fine.

She had figured it out about four months in.

She had not, at the time, set out to figure it out. The figuring-out had arrived the way conclusions arrived to her — slowly, while her hands were doing something else. She had been on Maeve, recalibrating his lateral array for the seventh time, and Kyle had said something — she could not now remember what; the *what* had not been the point — and she had glanced up at his face, and the face had done the thing it did, which was *not* the cataloging, was something else, and she had thought, with the small clear startle that was her only mode of intuition:

*Oh. He likes me. He likes me back.*

And then, two seconds behind it, the harder thought:

*And he is keeping the distance on purpose.*

She had finished the calibration. She had said nothing. She had walked Kyle to the door. She had closed her own door behind him. She had stood in her unit with the music down and run, in her head, the inventory of every small thing about him she had ever filed, and had matched each small thing to the new framework, and the framework had held — the way a *good* framework held, where the data did not have to be coerced; the data simply *fit.*

Kyle did not allow people close to him because *people close to him were used.* It was not a guess. It was the entire shape of his life. The corundum strop. The flat voice. The cataloging eyes. The eleven-beat footfall measured because measuring was what you did when you had decided, somewhere along the way, that nobody could afford to know your tells. He had not invented the rule that closeness was weakness; he had *paid* for the rule. The price had been someone, or several someones, who had not made it.

He had decided, a long time before her, that he would not make her one of the someones.

She had stood in the unit and let the framework settle.

She had not, the surprise of her own life, felt rejected.

She had felt — *seen,* she thought, and the *seen* was not from him; the *seen* was from herself; she had finally seen the shape of what she had walked into, and the shape was not a smaller life than she'd thought, and it was not a larger one, it was *exactly the size* of the life she had — and she had thought, plainly: *I can live in this. This is a life. He is across the hall. I am here. We will both still be here on Tuesday.*

She had named the framework on the brick wall. Small. Bottom corner. Where she could see it every morning.

*The asymmetry holds. The asymmetry is not the wound.*

Under it, two days later, she had added: *The wound is mine. The boots are mine. The unit is mine. He is across the hall, and he is across the hall on purpose. He will be there tomorrow. So will I.*

Nobody else had ever read the wall. The wall was for her.

The roof was, currently, for her too.

She took a sip of the coffee. The coffee was bad in the specific way only coffee made by yourself in your own unit at 0600 on a Sunday in October could be bad — meaning, in some private reading, *perfect.* She set the mug down on the bench. She picked the iron back up. She had a board to finish for a man on the third floor who needed it back by morning. The third-floor man's name was Berto. Berto had a daughter who was thirteen and was learning, slowly, badly, with much delight, how to play a cracked plastic flute that Pixel had repaired twice. The flute would need a third repair within a year. Pixel would do the third repair. The flute did not yet know.

She worked. The light moved.

The ferrocement wave to the west caught the sun at the exact angle that meant the day was about to change registers — coral becoming gold, gold becoming the long flat afternoon — and the city under it was a thing she had once arrived in at seventeen with a bag of tools and a pair of boots that didn't fit, and which, she registered, six years and change later, had not killed her, had not even *meaningfully* hurt her, had instead given her —

A list. *I have a list,* she thought, without writing it down, because the wall already had it.

*A unit. A workbench named Maeve. A song from before the Centennial. The boots. The brass-handled probe. The diagnostic clip from a stranger named Auntie. A jar of pickled cucumbers, replenished every six weeks by Mrs. Eldering, who was now ninety-one and considered Pixel her granddaughter without telling her so. A flute belonging to a thirteen-year-old. A landlord whose favor was now my responsibility to know without being told. A man across the hall.*

*A door. Unlocked.*

She smiled. Just a little. Just for herself.

A pigeon — flattered, gilded — landed on the parapet four feet from her bench. The pigeon was magnificent. The pigeon had a small piece of plastic in its beak that it was going to weave into its nest, because GLMZ pigeons did not understand that some things were not nest material and had decided, at some point in their species' tenure here, that they did not have to.

*Defiance,* Pixel thought, watching the pigeon. *That is what defiance looks like. It looks like an idiot bird with the wrong material.*

She finished the solder. She set the iron in the stand. She picked up her coffee. She watched the light.

Downstairs, in 2F, the unit was empty. The unit would not be empty by tomorrow. Pixel would know within ninety seconds.

In 2E, Maeve was waiting. Maeve always waited. Maeve was the patient member of the household.

The wall, Pixel thought, would have something new to add tonight. It always did.

She drank the coffee. The coffee was bad. The roof was hers. The city was hers in the specific way the city *let* a person have it, which was not really at all, but in the moment, was *enough.*

She was, she registered, not doing this badly.

She was, in fact, doing it on purpose.

She sat with the iron and the coffee and the gilded pigeon and the song from before the Centennial in both ears, and watched October light hit a city that had tried to be unkind to her, and had failed.
